paragraphs.text: From this passage we get some impression of the inward exercises of Paul. In this little company together here today there are many inward feelings and exercises. The Lord knows at this moment the exercises that we have. How much love we have enjoyed from Him! What a heart do we know in our blessed Lord Jesus! It is today and at all times towards us. We are always under His eye, and in His heart we have each one a place. It has often been said, but it should be apprehended in its fulness and attraction, that we have a place in the Lord’s heart, and the enemy can never rob us of it. Paul had a lasting impression of the Lord. Love flows towards us from His heart; it cannot be easily expressed in words, but must be experienced. I would like to emphasize this for the young ones. You are loved with a love that is eternal.
This can never change because it abides for ever in the heart of the Lord Jesus Himself.

We learn much in his writings of the inward exercises of Paul who, although an apostle, speaks as a man who had a history with God. How much is written in books about human thoughts, but the question is, what is my experience with God? What have I learned from the Son and the Spirit? Oh how wonderful is the assembly and every opportunity we have of meeting together! We receive an impression from the Lord, again and again a fresh impression. We gain something we have not experienced in just the same way before; it is quite new in this respect—a fresh experience with the Lord,
the Son of God, in the place where He now is. Perhaps it is an impression of the love of the Father for the Son, or of the Son for the Father. The power of the Spirit comes into this.

Without the voice of the Spirit we would never understand it; it becomes something wonderful and living in the assembly. I ask myself today whether I have freshly experienced the Spirit’s voice. How powerfully, clearly, and attractively it comes to us in the assembly and brings us into the realization of our relationship with Christ, and with the Father as His sons.
What is my history with God? The apostle shows us that he had had a place among men.

What a personality he was, and what a man in Judaism! He does not speak proudly about it, but he did have a history among men. Why does he speak of it? In order to show that all this was finished with. He had been on the Damascus road and had seen the Lord, who had asked him why he was occupied as he was. He says later that what had been gain to him he now counted as loss. No matter what it was that had made him proud, or distinguished him in the eyes of men, it was all loss. Perhaps we love our work. Does mine interest me too much? I ask myself. Is it gain to me or loss? Paul came to it that it was all loss. Each one of us has had something which we have learned to describe as loss.

In the assembly the test is whether the truth is being maintained. The Lord loves us so much that He proves us as to whether all is for His pleasure. Such is His love for the assembly that He will have nothing in it that hinders. The assembly is the vessel that affords response to His heart. The Lord loved Paul, but would never take pleasure in what was of the old man. It is necessary that we come to an understanding of this through the excellency of the knowledge of Christ

Jesus as Lord. At what a cost I now have the knowledge of Christ Jesus as Lord! It has cost His death, all the pain and suffering, in order that I should have this knowledge, the excellency of the knowledge of such a Person. Is it not something wonderful? What a glorious Lord we have in Jesus! For His sake Paul suffered loss and counted all as filth. What exercises were his! Our own exercises must be definite, and the Lord would strengthen them with us. Paul the Pharisee, that great man, was no more; all was ended for Paul in death at the cross. He has now a goal before him and speaks quite plainly about it. He speaks of righteousness by faith, as in the letter to the Romans. He speaks of the fellowship of Christ’s sufferings in the testimony. We suffer together with the Lord as sharing His reproach. The Lord was crucified, so we seek no place in the world in which He was crucified.

Paul says moreover, “Not that I have already obtained the prize ... but I pursue”. He had been taken possession of by the Lord, not by violence, but in His love. Paul could now do nothing of his own will, he was—and we are to be—taken possession of by the Lord. “I pursue” means that he had not reached the goal. Perhaps we may say, ‘I have reached the goal; I am there’. But no, there is always more; we are not there yet; even if we have great knowledge there is more to be learned of Jesus.
The Lord is coming quickly, but whilst we are still in the wilderness there is always something fresh for us. What is our objective? That is a question I should often ask myself.

“Forgetting the things behind ... I pursue”; and Paul’s goal is Christ. Have you or I a different one? Let us take up the challenge and answer it. Have I a different goal from Paul? We all have exercises, but our goal must be that of Paul. His objective must be mine, and no other. “And if ye are any otherwise minded, this also God shall reveal to you”—what grace! He will not forsake us; He knows our exercises and will make all clear to us. We may always seek the Lord as we judge ourselves and enjoy communion with Him; we ask and He answers. It is a living system in which we know what glory is. It is important that we tread together such a path as Paul found. Let us walk in the same steps. What a path!—our goal the Lord Jesus, the One well-pleasing to God and exalted by Him.

I draw attention to this scripture very briefly. At the last care meeting we were challenged as to whether there was manliness among us. Almost immediately the Lord has put in the midst of our hearts and affections, interests and concern, a little child. I raise the question with myself as to whether the Lord has something to say to us in that.

I do not say in any way that manliness and the little child are incompatible, or that there is one over against the other. I believe that the characteristics of a little child are also the characteristics of manliness. The disciples to whom Jesus gave this object-lesson here were all men, they were all grown-up. They were child ish

at the beginning of the chapter. They were striving as to who should be greatest, and that is a childish, characteristic. Characteristics of childishness are never attractive. The characteristics of what is child like are to be amongst us, and I have wondered whether the Lord, having worked in His own way to draw our attention to one of our little children, is not desirous of saying something to us again that regard. I do not expand on it. I think it would require more experience of the quality than perhaps I have to be able to expand on it. Much has been said about it in ministry which we can read, and there are things about it that we can repeat, but the question is, Who actually knows it? Who has been converted? Has anyone been converted? That is the question.

I was thinking the other Lord’s day, when I was preaching somewhere, as to how many of us have actually had the experience of being converted, and I venture to think not all. The gospel becomes accepted because we have grown up in it, but we need to be converted, and we do not need only to be converted as being sinners; we need to be converted to be as little children. The suggestion is that we are not naturally like it, that qualities that characterize us are not like this, and Jesus says, “Unless ye are converted, and become as little children”. He set the little child in their midst. He would give them an example and a demonstration. It is a very challenging question—If Jesus wanted to do this tonight who could He choose? Could He bring forward and say, Here is a little child? as we go back to the beginning of this gospel we find that in a sense it is Himself, because over and over again we have references to the little Child. Then it is interesting that Matthew 17, out of which this flows, ends with “me and thee”, and the ‘Me’ is the little Child; and is the ‘thee’ a little child? The Lord is saying,

Unless you are converted and become like that … It is related here to entering the kingdom. It is in its own setting in this gospel, in the setting of the kingdom. It is also, we may say, in the setting of the assembly.

It would be interesting to trace the way in which Jesus in some sense delineates the way in which He will build the assembly from Matthew 16, where evidently the assembly is not in existence and He says He will build it, to chapter 18 where it is in existence and can be spoken to. Several things come in between. There is His own glory and our association with Him in it, and there is the spirit of the little child, as if that would characterise the assembly.

Think of what it means, what it lays the foundation for. We think of Solomon: God asked him what he would like and he said he was but a little child, and he did not know how to go out or how to come in (see 1 Kings 3: 7), and on the basis of that he was given wisdom. It was on the basis of his taking this ground, you might say this converted ground, that he was given wisdom to judge that great people, and in the millennial day the little child will lead all kinds of disparate elements and lead them in peace. They will not hurt or destroy in all God’s holy mountain (see Isaiah 11: 6, 9 and 65: 25).

I just leave this with the brethren. The point has been very much in my mind as we have thought of our young brother who is now in hospital, the object of our prayers and attention and affection. It is as if the Lord would draw our attention to it. We think of him in many ways. If I could refer to him personally, his brightness among us and his friendliness, and the way in which he would go round the brethren and speak to everybody, and speak to everybody cheerfully and friendlily. What an example of a little child! Beloved, the Lord would

not have allowed this at this particular time, I think, if He did not want to say something to us. Therefore let us consider whether we have been converted, and in that sense whether we could be made an example of as Jesus made an example of this little child in this particular chapter.

articles.title: ABIDING WITH THE LORD
articles.author: A. B. Parker
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Brooklyn, N.Y.

paragraphs.text: I had the sense that the Lord brought this passage of Scripture to my attention today and I therefore venture to speak of it. It has occurred to me that Saul of Tarsus may be spoken of as the New Testament counterpart of Mephibosheth, who referred to himself as a dead dog.
Saul, who also is Paul, said that he was the first of sinners. Both had a tremendous sense of having the mercy of God shown them. Paul spoke about himself as seeing himself as God had seen him.

It says of Barnabas that he was a good man; indeed he was a prince having been given a title by the apostles—son of consolation. We may wonder what need there would be for consolation at the beginning when the twelve apostles were present and there was such unity and unselfishness amongst the disciples. But in the presence of all that Barnabas rose to the dignity of being called a son of consolation. Why? Perhaps because he took on the ministry.
He certainly took on the spirit and character of the dispensation. He sold his lands,

coming into the full light of God’s mind for the Levites. No sacrifice would be too great; he was wholeheartedly in the good of the heavenly inheritance. He brought the money he received for his property and laid it at the feet of the apostles. He contributed to the existing oneness. Later, he is referred to as an apostle—“the apostles Barnabas and Paul”, Acts 14: 14.
Truly, he was a prince.

In Acts 13: 1, it says, “Now there were in Antioch, in the assembly which was there, prophets and teachers—Barnabas ...”. Barnabas is named first. Earlier, he had gone to search out Saul of Tarsus to bring him to Antioch. Why did he do that? I believe he realized that he faced a very difficult situation there at Antioch. Some may say, Why? Things were prospering; people were getting blessing in multitudes. Yes, but who were they? They were Gentiles; persons who, in practice and general manner of life, had been far off from God without any knowledge of the truth. Think of such persons being brought, through the glad tidings, into the assembly! What a vibrantly happy people they would be! But think of the teaching they would need! It says later that for a whole year they were taught. So you can see how Barnabas felt he needed help in this. It is evident that he realized that here was a situation with which he could not cope alone, and so he went to search out Saul. But before he went, he exhorted these new disciples “with purpose of heart to abide with the Lord”. That is a very remarkable expression. He knew that teaching was needed, but, firstly, they were to come to know the One in whom they had believed—not only objectively, but experimentally, through abiding with Him. One of the sweetest stories in the Old Testament is of a young woman who clave to Naomi, a godly woman who had brought to her the knowledge of God. It says that she clave to Naomi, and that she lodged with Naomi. It implies a very close relationship; it is a heart matter—with purpose of heart. I would suggest that if we abide with the Lord He will see to it that we will find direction from Him as to what we should do in times of crisis.
Naomi said to Ruth, “Shall I not seek rest for thee?” (Ruth 3: 1). And the Lord Jesus said,
“Where I am, there also shall be my servant”, John 12: 26. Beloved brethren, we want to be with Him.

Well, this was a difficult situation which faced Barnabas. This crowd of buoyant, freshly converted persons had left the things to which they had been accustomed. They needed teaching; they needed food; they needed encouragement; they needed to be built up; they needed to be told about the inheritance. And, dear brethren, we need all these things, but we need teaching—and to appropriate teaching. For many years many of us had good teaching; we thought we were in the good of what was ministered, but later, very quickly we were diverted from the good teaching. Beloved brethren, we need to abide with the Teacher! “They said to him, Rabbi (which ... signifies Teacher), where abidest thou? He says to them, Come and see”, John 1: 38. It is not alone a question of how much we know, or how well we may quote Scripture; that has its place; but behind it all there is the need for having purpose of heart to abide with the Lord. Barnabas could not have served those hew converts better than to exhort them to abide with the Lord. It is the only way to be kept from stumbling; “But to him that is able to keep you without stumbling”, Jude 24. One would just seek to strengthen the confidence of the brethren in this personal relationship with the Lord Jesus, that we may take in right teaching, and live it.

After this whole year of teaching at Antioch these two ministering brothers were taken away from the brethren in Antioch to serve elsewhere. Would the instructed ones they left behind go on in fidelity? If they remembered the exhortation of Barnabas to abide with the Lord, they would be true to what they had been taught. We hear of serious decline when Paul left Corinth, but there is no intimation that it was so at Antioch. The Lord can have confidence in His people if they are abiding with Him.

But one more comment on Saul of Tarsus—in Acts 13: 1, where we have the list of those who were ministering to the Lord and fasting, Saul’s name appears last. That was after he had been teaching with Barnabas for a whole year. But that was the way he served. He did not complain that his name was last. He said that he was least of all the apostles. He was so like Mephibosheth—“Let Ziba take all”, 2 Samuel 19: 30.

Well, dear brethren, that is just what one had in mind. My concern for myself and for my brethren is that in these difficult days we may be kept abiding with the Lord. It requires purpose of heart, but He will see to it that what is approved of Him will be preserved and kept in the way everlasting—in the way of righteousness. May we all be: kept thus, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: THE NEED OF FAITH
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Brooklyn, N.Y.

paragraphs.speaker: E. E.
paragraphs.text: Hoyte *
2 Thessalonians 1: 3–6

I have been thinking of this Thessalonian assembly, this locality, and what was in it, of which the apostle takes account and speaks. They had qualities that increased. Paul says, “Your faith increases exceedingly, and the love of each one of you all towards one another abounds”—
remarkable! I was thinking much of the sifting that is proceeding at the present time. Our brother touched upon the sickness among us, and so on.

This assembly had a good start, an excellent start: they “turned to God from idols to serve a living and true God, and to await his Son from the heavens”, 1 Thessalonians 1: 9. The first chapter of the second epistle shows these same conditions, faith proceeding with them, happy conditions, loving one another. This matter of faith, dear brethren; I feel we need it. It was disbelief in those persons of whom our first brother read in Numbers 14. They disbelieved God; they did not believe that God could carry them through; it was lack of faith. But Caleb was a man rich in faith; he had a store-house of it. He said, “Jehovah is with us”.

The tests we are going through are kind of keen, and they are sifting us. Believe it or not, in our localities we are being sifted. I do not know how you regard it, but the Lord is thinking of us. He said to Peter, “Satan has demanded to have you, to sift you as wheat; but I have besought for thee”, Luke 22: 31, 32. That is the word; the
* with Christ July 1980
sifting was going on in them all, in all the apostles, but the Lord said, “I have besought for thee that thy faith fail not”. How quickly Peter was recovered—he went out and wept bitterly.

Some of us do not see our errors; we refuse to adjust them, to think about them; we just shake it off. Peter went out and wept bitterly. It says, “The Lord is indeed risen and has appeared to Simon”, Luke 24: 34. The Lord had said, “I have besought for thee”. Dear brethren, the Lord has us in mind in this sifting. Are we qualified, are we equal to it? We need faith. That is what the Lord says to Peter. He did not say he was not a follower. Peter said, ‘I will die for you’. ‘You will die for Me?—The cock shall not crow today before you have denied Me thrice’. Peter intended to do it, you know; he drew his sword; but he was in a position in which he was weak. The Lord was facing death; how much the Lord faced; only He could face it, dear brethren—and He says, “I have besought for thee”.

I just thought of adding a word to what our dear brethren have been saying in relation to faith and love. We see the condition of this assembly, this locality. Paul says, “We ought to thank God always for you because your faith increases”; notice that. If you looked in the first epistle you would find in the first chapter “We give thanks to God always for you all, making mention of you at our prayers, remembering unceasingly your work of faith, and labour of love, and enduring constancy of hope” (1 Thessalonians 1: 2, 3). Now the thing is that they continued; they did not retrograde. But they were being tested; in this epistle a dark background of apostasy sets in. But here is a local company that is in the gain of faith. There is a little weakness with them; it seems as if they were misdirected in some way; at any rate they were being tested and the sifting was proceeding. The apostle says, “We ought to thank God always for you”.

I stop, but I just wanted to bring the idea of faith in, dear brethren. At one time the apostles said to the Lord, “Give more faith to us” (Luke 17: 5); they felt the need of it. How much more we do, dear brethren, in these times. This second epistle is something to consider—what is being restrained, and what is going to be taken out of the way to open up the whole channel of evil, when the lawless one shall be revealed. But with faith on our part, the Lord will bring us through. He says, “I also will keep thee out of the hour of trial”, Revelation 3: 10. So we need faith. May the Lord help us.

I had in mind to speak about the need for us to appreciate what is small. It is the very condition into which our Lord came. He came not only into manhood’s condition but He came in the form of a Babe; what compression! That is what I would like to encourage our hearts about, dear brethren, that what is small does not mean that it is feeble; what is small does not mean that it is weak; but the acceptance of smallness makes room for us to prove the power of God. They were too big at Corinth, you know. Paul had difficulty in getting in at Corinth. They were too big; he said that; they had been reigning (see 1 Corinthians 4: 8). I think there is a need for us to be small in our

own eyes. One man in the Old Testament had a time when he was like that and God looked on him, and God had something in him, I believe; it says, “when thou wast little in thine eyes”, 1 Samuel 15: 17. It is an attitude that we need to keep, of being small, and yet in that smallness we have in mind the whole scope of divine things.

The verse in Isaiah speaks of a residue or a remnant and we have been taught that a remnant has all the features of the whole, save in the quantity of it. So in those small conditions there are all the features of the assembly. Two in a place, gathering together, small outward conditions, yet there are all the features of the assembly. Let us have a right view of what is small. It is not that we are so small that we are careless; it is not that we have become small and things do not matter. So if it is only two or three in a place they are together in the light of the whole, and what regulates the assembly of God would regulate a few together in smallness in a place.

I believe we need to be helped, as I have said; though it be a remnant it is a small piece of the whole with all the characteristics of the whole, the same quality. The quality is not any less because it is the end piece; the warmth, the substantiality of what is there is just the same. So may we be helped as we come together in smallness. There may be just two or three in a place, yet what is there has the characteristics of the assembly of God in that place; so they gather together to pray, they gather together for the Lord’s supper. As together, if we have this attitude, we have a sense that we are a part of the whole. The whole assembly is not there, the whole is not to be seen in two or three persons, but the characteristics of the whole are there in a few gathered together “unto my name”, Matthew 18: 20. So let us not despise the smallness,

or be discouraged by it either, because I think if there is the right attitude with us as we come together the Lord and the Spirit would quickly give us a touch that we belong to Christ, we are part of His heavenly bride.

In Isaiah I only wanted to touch on God’s sovereignty experienced in small conditions; it says, “Unless Jehovah of hosts had left us a very small residue”. We may even boast, you know, in smallness; maybe we could boast that we are among those who have stood for things; I do not think we shall get the Lord’s help on that line. It says, “Unless Jehovah of hosts ...”; He has been sovereign in the way He has helped us through. It is God’s own distinct operation that He has preserved a remnant that is left. What a company to be in, the remnant that is left! They are going to be awakened; how encouraging Isaiah is in the later chapters—“Arise, shine! for thy light is come” (Isaiah 60: 1)—what a word to the remnant!

What a word to a few in a place—“Arise, shine! for thy light is come, and the glory of Jehovah is risen upon thee”. Well, God’s sovereignty enters into all that. As we fall back on what God has done in His own sovereign operations, ways that we could not trace, we see there are other persons who have been more faithful perhaps than ourselves, more devoted, and yet they may not be remembering the Lord today. Well, “Unless Jehovah of hosts had left us a very small residue, we should have been as Sodom, we should have been like unto Gomorrah”. But God in His own sovereign way has preserved us. May we appreciate His ways in sovereign mercy. Paul appreciated them, and as He appreciated them he said, “How unsearchable his judgments, and untraceable his ways!”, Romans 11: 55. Well, I think that is one thing that a sense of smallness would cause us to appreciate—God’s own ways in sovereign mercy.
Another thing that is connected with smallness is wisdom, as we would see in Proverbs. I think the Corinthians, as I said, were too big to be wise, they were wise in their own eyes.

Solomon says there are four things little upon the earth and they are exceeding wise. This attitude that I have spoken of makes room for divine wisdom. If there are a few of us in a place in the light of the whole assembly, who else than Christ can we turn to for direction?

Who else can give us help to work out right principles? Certainly not anyone that is near by us who is walking in a path of self-will, not even persons who may have helped us in former years. I think the sense of littleness would cause us to be cast on divine wisdom. It is one of the things that Christ has been made to us; “who has been made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and holiness, and redemption”, 1 Corinthians 1: 30. He has been “made to us”; that would be the small people; He has been made to us wisdom from God. Well, there is a need for wisdom among us, I think any right-minded person would feel that, and here Solomon sees some things little upon the earth and they are exceeding wise. Where did they learn it? There could not have been room in the systems of men for these things, the ants, the rock-badgers, the locusts, and the lizard; there could not have been room in the systems of men to educate these. They would be characteristic of persons, and yet they were exceeding wise.
Where was their wisdom? Our wisdom is in falling back on the God who has sovereignly chosen us, as Jacob did on “the God that shepherded me all my life long”, Genesis 48: 15.

Jacob was some time coming to it but he became an exceedingly wise man. He could bless the greatest monarch of the time; he was a man who had journeyed on his own way at one time, but he became dependent, he had his name changed, and became exceeding wise. Paul is
another; Paul proved wisdom; he learned it through being lowered through a wall in a basket.

What a humiliating experience for a learned man of the world! But you see the learning of the world would not have saved him when the gates of the city were being watched day and night and they were ready to slay him; what saved him was “another way”.

I thought of that passage in Matthew, “take to thee the little child and his mother” (see Matthew 2: 13), as “another way”. As we embrace divine things there is a whole system of heavenly administration available that we might be exceeding wise. Herod was set for the destruction of the child Jesus; all the resources of the world were set against Christ; but there was “another way” as Joseph listened to wisdom. He was small enough to do as he was told; that was wisdom—the fear of the Lord the beginning of wisdom—and he was small enough to do it. He might well have reasoned a lot of things in those early chapters in Matthew. I think Joseph represents to us a man who was small in his own eyes, and he was exceeding wise. Think of all the resources that Herod had being thwarted as they sought the child Jesus; there was “another way”; the magi departed “another way”, Matthew 2: 12. Those men were exceeding wise, but small, little upon the earth. May that attitude mark us increasingly, that we make way for divine wisdom, divine resources.

As I have said, in Corinth it was hard, it took a long time; Paul said, “there is not a wise person among you, not even one” (1 Corinthians 6: 5); they were too big. There was a lot of man’s wisdom, and it comes in among us; it is very near to us; we are very apt to fall back on it; maybe if isolated from our brethren we are very apt to fall back on the wisdom of the world and bring disaster and sorrow and distress. But if we are small

enough, dear brethren, in our own eyes the God who has redeemed us will see us through, and we shall come in for the resources of wisdom. It reminds us of Daniel; the wisdom of that man, who fed on pulse and water, was far greater than all the learning of the day; he was exceeding wise. He was content to be little, he was content not to have a name here but to draw his resources from someone else; he knew the companionship of the Son of God. “Go thy way until the end; and thou shalt ... stand in thy lot at the end of the days”, Daniel 12: 13.
There is a man who was little upon the earth and he was exceeding wise. He saw one king go and another come. God is going to see us through, dear brethren.

That is why I read in Hebrews that there is a line that He is seeing through; it says, “for he has prepared for them a city”. God is going to house His own work in His own environment, in His own arrangement. Well we may feel put out oft-times; we may feel that the small line is not gaining any ground; but God is going to see it through. These persons in this chapter—

the apostle says time would fail to speak of them—God saw them through; He not only saw them through but He is going to house them; it says, “he has prepared for them a city”. What a city, it will be, dear brethren. Abraham will be there, all these persons in this chapter will be there. What a valuation God has of these persons, small upon the earth, despised among the, nations; as they sought to be true to the God who had chosen them, they would be set at nought by men; but God has prepared for them a city. Oh may we appreciate the God who comforts us in these small circumstances; the God who comes down to these small details and exercises of our pathway; He has prepared for us a city. These small conditions are preparing us for the city, preparing us to learn wisdom, because in that city you are meant to function, you know; there will be no suburban dwellers in that
city, every one in that city will be functioning as having learned divine wisdom and appreciated divine sovereignty.

May we grow in the appreciation of these things, so that, as we come to appreciate what God has done, in that day we shall fill out our place; “he has prepared for them a city”. In that city, as I said, each will function in his own formation, formation that is taking place now in small conditions; but, may I say in closing that in the present small conditions there is to be a representation of the whole in its true character, for His name’s sake.
Beloved Brethren and Sisters in Christ,

The day of the apostasy is hastening on with rapid strides, and also the day in which the Lord shall come to snatch His own away. The present moment is of so solemn a character that I feel constrained to address you this word of exhortation. Godly men everywhere, who watch the signs of the times, see the moment approaching which shall terminate the present actings of grace. The time has evidently arrived when one must speak plainly and, decisively, and ask you where you are, and what you are about. You have by grace, which has shone brighter and brighter as it has approached its termination, been gathered out of the seething mass of idolatry and wickedness which now threatens

Christendom and the world with an overthrow more awful than that of Sodom and Gomorrah of old; and the question is whether you are adequately impressed with the responsibility, as well as the blessedness, of the ground you are on, and walking like men and women whose eyes have been opened.

Believe me, there has never been in the world’s history such a time as the present, and Satan is occupied with none as he is with you; and his occupation with you is the more to be feared because of the subtlety of his operations. His object is to withdraw your attention from Christ, while you suppose you are on safe ground and have nothing to fear. He would destroy you with the very truth itself. For mark the subtlety—you are on safe ground but only while Christ is your all in all. Here is where Satan is drawing some away. Interpose anything between your soul and Christ, and your Philadelphia becomes Laodicea; your safe ground is as unsafe as the rest of Christendom; your strength is gone from you, and you become weak, like any ordinary mortal. Some of you are young, recently converted, or brought to the right ways of the Lord, and you do not know the depths of Satan. But you are hereby solemnly warned of your peril; and if mischief overtake you, you cannot plead ignorance.

Again I say, Satan has his eye specially upon you, for the purpose of interposing the world in some form between your soul and Christ. He cares not how little, or in what form. If you knew but how little will answer his purpose, you would be alarmed. It is not by that which is gross or shameful; such is the development, not the beginning of evil. It is not by anything glaring that he seeks to ruin you, but in small and seemingly harmless trifles—trifles that would not shock nor offend anyone as things go, and yet these constitute the deadly and insidious poison, destined to ruin

your testimony and withdraw you from Christ. Do you ask what are these alarming symptoms, and where are they seen? The question does but show what is the character of the opiate at work. Brethren and sisters, you are being infected with the spirit of the world. Your dress, your manner, your talk, your lack of spirituality, betray it in every gathering. There is a dead weight, a restraint, a want of power, that reveals itself in the meetings, as plainly as if your heart were visibly displayed and its thoughts publicly read. A form of godliness without power is beginning to be seen among you, as plainly as in Christendom generally.

As surely as you tamper with the world, so surely will you drift away to its level. This is the nature of things. It must be so. If you tamper with the world, the privileged place you occupy, instead of shielding you, will only expose you to greater condemnation. It must be Christ or the world. It cannot be—ought not to be—Christ and the world. God’s grace in drawing you out of the world in your ignorance is one thing, but God will never permit you to prostitute His grace, and play fast and loose, when you have been separated from the world. Remember you take the place, and claim the privilege, of one whose eyes have been opened; and if on the one hand this is unspeakably blessed (and it is), on the other hand it is the most dreadful position in which a human being can be found. It is to be at the wedding feast without the wedding garment. ‘It is to say, “Lord, Lord”, while you do not the things that He bids. It is to say, “I go, sir”, as he said who went not.

Beloved, I am persuaded better things of you, though I thus speak; and I have confidence in you, in the Lord, that you will bless Him for these few faithful words. Nothing can be more glorious than the position you are called to occupy in these

closing days. Saints have stood in the breach, have watched through weary days and nights these eighteen hundred years, and, you only wait for the trumpet of victory to go in and take possession of the glorious inheritance. Other men laboured, and ye are entered into their labours; and yet, forsooth, you are lowering your dignity to the level of the poor potsherds of the earth, who only wait for the rod of the Victor (and yours too) to be dashed into pieces.

Oh, awake, then from your lethargy—slumber no longer; put away your idols and false gods; wash your garments, and get you to Bethel, where you will find God to be better than ever you knew Him, even in your best days. Lay aside your last bit of worldly dress; guard your speech, that it be of Christ and His affairs, and not, as you know it now often is, of anything but Him. Let your prayers mingle with those of other saints at the prayer meetings; they never were more needed. Neglect no opportunity of gathering up instruction from that word which alone can keep us from the paths of the destroyer, and let your life be the evidence of the treasures you gather up at the lecture, or the reading-meeting, or in secret with the Lord. If you want occupation, with a glorious reward from a beloved Master, ask that Master to set you to work for Him—you will never regret it, either in this world or in that which is to come.

Beloved, bear with me; I am jealous over you with godly jealousy. You belong to Christ, and Christ to you. Break not this holy union. Let not the betrothed one be unfaithful to her Bridegroom! Why should you be robbed and spoiled? And for what? Empty husks and bitter fruits, while you waste this little span of blessing! All the distinctions acquired here in the energy of the Spirit will but serve to enhance your beauty and render you more lovely in the eyes of Him who has espoused you to Himself. Can you refuse Him His delights in you? Can you refuse Him the fruit of the travail of His soul, who once hung, a dying man, between two thieves, on Calvary, a spectacle to men and angels, and for you—you who have forgotten (for you cannot have despised) this devotedness for you. He could have taken the world without the cross, and left you out, but He would not; and now will you, having been enriched by those agonies and that blood, take the world into your tolerance and leave Him out? Impossible! Your pure mind did but need to be stirred up by way of remembrance.

Let us therefore take courage from this moment. We have lately been, offering up prayers, confessing the lack of piety and devotedness. May we not take this word as the answer of our ever-gracious faithful Lord, to arouse us—to re-awaken our drooping energies? And then the more quickly He comes the better. We shall not be ashamed before Him at His coming.
(This word was reprinted in ‘The Believer’s Friend’ in 1926 and again in ‘Words of Truth’ in 1953).

Naaman had to learn the great lesson of the ways of God in death; he had to face death; and no one is of value in the service of God unless he faces this great question of death. Naaman went down into Jordan and plunged seven times, and “his flesh became again like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean”. If every one had the flesh of a little child there would never be a cause of sorrow to our brethren, or a dishonour to God.
